title: Human vectors and social engineering
prompt: During awareness training, employees review recent social engineering attempts against the company. Match each human vector to the description that fits it. One description will not be used.

pairs.why: Vishing is voice phishing: the lure arrives as a call or voicemail.

pairs.right: Text message with a fake delivery link
pairs.why: Smishing is SMS phishing: the lure arrives as a text message.

pairs.right: Compromising a site the targets often visit
pairs.why: The attacker infects a third-party site the target group trusts and waits for victims to come to it.
Typosquatting relies on users mistyping or misreading a URL, landing on the attacker's domain.

pairs.right: Invented scenario to justify a request
pairs.why: Pretexting is the fabricated story (an audit, an urgent vendor issue) that makes the request seem legitimate.

pairs.right: Hijacked executive mailbox requests a wire
pairs.why: BEC uses a compromised or spoofed legitimate business account, often to redirect payments.

explanation: Vishing and smishing are defined by the channel, watering hole and typosquatting by where the victim is lured, pretexting by the story, and BEC by the abuse of a trusted business mailbox. The unused description is disinformation, which is a separate human vector.

title: Identify the malware from its behavior
prompt: An incident responder is summarizing findings from several malware cases. Classify each observed behavior by the type of malware it MOST likely indicates. One type will not be used.

items.text: Encrypts file shares and demands payment
items.why: Holding data hostage for payment is the defining trait of ransomware.

items.text: Spreads host to host via an SMB flaw, no clicks
items.why: Self-propagation across the network without user action is a worm.

items.text: Infects an executable; runs when the user opens it
items.why: Attaching to a host file and needing user execution to spread is a virus.

items.text: Free PDF converter that secretly opens a backdoor
items.why: Malicious code disguised as legitimate software is a Trojan.

items.text: Wipes payroll DB once its author's account is disabled
items.why: Dormant code that fires when a specific condition is met is a logic bomb.

items.text: Modifies the kernel to hide its files and processes
items.why: Concealing itself at a privileged level to evade detection is a rootkit.

explanation: Focus on the distinguishing behavior: worms self-propagate while viruses need a host file and user action; Trojans rely on disguise; logic bombs wait for a trigger (date, event, account change); rootkits hide at the kernel or firmware level; ransomware extorts through encryption; keyloggers capture input, but no behavior here describes one, so Keylogger is unused. Rootkits often require reimaging because the infected OS cannot be trusted to report on itself.

title: Assessment findings and mitigation techniques
prompt: A security manager is triaging findings from a recent assessment. Match each finding to the mitigation technique that BEST addresses it. One technique will not be used.

pairs.left: Kiosk PCs run portable, unapproved executables
pairs.why: Only an allow list blocks execution of anything not explicitly approved, including portable apps that need no installation rights.

pairs.left: IoT cameras share a flat network with finance
pairs.why: Placing the cameras in their own segment (VLAN/subnet with filtering) stops them from reaching finance systems.

pairs.left: Retired file server is still online
pairs.why: A system with no business purpose should be formally decommissioned (data sanitized, removed from the network), not maintained.

pairs.left: Vendor fix exists for an exploited web CVE
pairs.why: When the vendor has released a fix for a known exploited flaw, applying the patch removes the vulnerability itself.

pairs.left: Help desk staff are domain administrators
pairs.why: Help desk tasks do not require domain admin rights; least privilege reduces them to only what the job needs.

pairs.left: Data on frequently lost laptops is readable
pairs.why: Full-disk encryption keeps data on a lost or stolen laptop confidential without the key.

explanation: Each finding has a root cause that one 2.5 technique removes directly: uncontrolled execution, a flat network, an unneeded asset, a known flaw, excessive rights and unprotected data at rest. Monitoring is detective; it would show the problems but would not BEST fix any of them.
